## Standard coding-agent procedure

1. Inspect `git status`, the relevant source files, tests, and this plan.
2. State the smallest proposed slice and any assumptions.
3. Implement without discarding unrelated changes.
4. Add focused tests, including failure branches where relevant.
5. Run focused tests.
6. Run the complete quality suite.
7. Review the diff and generated artifacts.
8. Report changed files, quality results, unresolved limitations, and the next slice.

## What it has

The core of the language, which reaches nothing outside the program:
records, functions (nested ones, closures, recursion within a stated
depth), `if`, `match`, `for`, `while`, `repeat`, `try`, `fail`, text with
values written in (`f"..."`), and the built-in methods on text, numbers,
lists, maps and optional values. Whole numbers are exact at any size.

It is held to the conformance suite in `../conformance`, where it must
print what the reference engine prints, word for word. See
`tests/test_conformance.py`.

## What it does not have yet

- **A checker.** The reference engine refuses a badly typed program before
  running it. This engine runs it, and fails later or not at all. Until it
  has one, do not trust it with a program the reference has not checked.
- Workflows, agents, tools, models, memories, boards, swarms and imports.
  A file that has one is refused, and the refusal names it.
- Tests that script a model's answers.
- Vectors and matrices.
- Traces and replay.

### The native engine lets an agent make its approved changes

- An agent's model may now ask for a tool that changes the world, in the
  native engine as in the reference (native/agent_changes.go). An agent
  that plans (`plan: first`, or by default when it has a model, a tool
  that changes something and two turns) shows all its changes as one
  plan; the run waits with exit code 3 for an approval of that plan, and
  begun again it is given back what its model said before, so the plan
  carried out is the one approved, in order. Changes asked for after the
  plan was carried out are told they cannot happen. An agent with `plan:
  off` may make one approved change a step; a second is refused. What the
  agent changed (`did`) is written from what ran.
- Held by `tests/test_conformance.py` with a stand-in model and the

result are recorded, `kosika story` lists them, and Studio shows each one as
it is made.

It can reach only the tools in `can`, and only as far as the person running
it granted. A look that fails, such as a file that is not there, is told to
the model so it can try something else. An answer given in plain words is
asked for once more as the record. A tool that changes something stops for
approval exactly as a direct call does; an agent may make one such change
per `ask` step. Asking for a tool it was never given ends the run.

This works with `--model-protocol ollama` and `openai`, on a model that was
trained to choose tools. A files tool with `operation: "peek"` reads only
the first 4000 characters, which suits a model reading for itself.

`}}` stand for one brace. It means exactly the same as joining the parts
  with `+`, and a program written either way has the same hash. An
  expression in braces MUST NOT contain a quotation mark or a brace.

- A workflow step MAY be `NAME = now` or `NAME = random LOW to HIGH`. `now`
  gives the built-in record `Moment {date: Text, time: Text, weekday: Text,
  year, month, day, hour, minute, epoch: Number}` in the host's local time.
  `random` gives `RandomNumber {value: Number}`, a whole number from LOW to
  HIGH inclusive; both MUST be whole numbers with LOW not above HIGH. Each
  is recorded in the trace as a read-only tool call (`clock_now`,
  `random_number`), so replay reads the recorded value. Neither needs a
  host grant. They MUST NOT appear inside a `fn`. A program that uses
  neither is unchanged and keeps its hash.

- A model step MAY be followed by `verify CHECK(arguments)`, written after
  the call and before any `vote` or `retry`:
  `found = use_model reader(p.text) verify proven(found, hits) retry 1`.
  CHECK MUST be a function declared in the program that returns Text. Its
  arguments may use the step's own name, which holds the model's answer, and

Declaring it reaches nothing. The person running the program names the sites
(`--allow-site en.wikipedia.org`, repeatable), and a fetch is refused unless
the address is on one of them.

What a fetch is, exactly:

* One GET of an `https` address on the standard port, to a named host that is
  an allowed site or a subdomain of one. No other scheme, no IP address, no
  user name or password in the address.
* Nothing is sent but the request itself: no cookies, no login, no form, no
  body. It cannot post, submit, or sign in to anything.
* A redirect is followed only to another allowed address, at most five times.
* At most 2 MiB is read, only `text/html` or `text/plain`, within 20 seconds.
* The page is reduced to its readable text, at most 20,000 characters, with
  scripts, styles, and markup removed. The address actually read is returned
  with it, so an answer can say where it came from.

A web page is written by a stranger and may contain text aimed at a model
("ignore your instructions and ..."). Kosika treats fetched text as data: it
is a `Text` value like any other, and a model that reads it in a thinking
step can only return that step's typed answer. It cannot call a tool, fetch
another page, or change anything because of what a page said. It can still
be fooled into a wrong answer, which is why the allowed sites are the
runner's choice and should be ones they trust.

An agent with `plan: first` MUST name a model, MUST be granted at least one
tool with `access: execute`, and MUST have `max_steps` of at least 2. Every

order and stop at the first failure. An `execute` call requested in a later
reply MUST NOT run; the model is told so as that call's result. When the step is resumed after
approval the model's earlier replies are replayed from the run's journal, not

### Host component contracts

`kosika.component/v1` is the supported host contract for binding a declared tool
to a local implementation artifact written in any language. It adds no new
Kosika syntax. A bound tool uses source `component:<component-id>`; its name,
operation, access label, generated input schema, and generated output schema MUST
exactly match the contract before execution.

The contract pins:

- semantic component version and tool identity;
- exact input and output JSON schemas;
- required effect and capability names;

Kosika starts that command itself, never through a shell, and keeps the
server running while Studio is open. The Tools page lists every granted
server with the tools it offers, and for each tool the Kosika text to paste
into a program. An agent given such tools in its `can` list is told what
they do in the server's own words and chooses among them.

The Skills page lists the skills kept beside each agent, in its `skills`
folder: what each is for, the words that pick it, and the rules it holds
files to. Type a request there to see which skills it would pick, and
why; no model is asked. A skill can be changed or a new one written on
the page. One that Kosika cannot read is not saved, and the page says why.

A tool may be `access: observe` only when the server itself marks it
read-only. Any other tool must be `access: execute`, so each use waits for
your Allow once. A tool that answers in plain text needs an output record
with one Text field. `examples/mcp` has a small notes server and an agent,
`librarian.kos`, that uses it.

A granted server runs with your authority. Grant only servers you trust.

Today there are two engines: the reference engine in `kosika/` (Python)
and the native engine in `native/` (Go). The native engine exists so that
Kosika can run on a machine with no Python.

## What is here

    cases/NAME.kos             a program whose tests must all pass
    cases/NAME.expected.txt    what `test` prints for it
    failing/NAME.kos           a program whose tests fail on purpose
    failing/NAME.expected.txt  what `test` prints for it, failures and all
    refused/NAME.kos           a program the checker must refuse
    refused/NAME.expected.txt  the one line `test` prints for it

Every program here is pure: records, functions and tests. It asks no
model, uses no tool and reaches no file, so it gives the same result on
any machine.

## What an engine must do

For each `.kos` file, `ENGINE test FILE` must print exactly the text in
the file beside it, and end with exit code 0 when every test passed, 1
when one failed, and 2 when the program was refused before it ran. A
refused program prints `Check failed: ` and the reason, and nothing else. Line ends may be `\n` or `\r\n`.

An engine must also split every `.kos` file in this repository into the
same tokens as the reference: `ENGINE tokens FILE` prints one JSON object
a line, `{"kind", "value", "line", "column"}`.

`tests/test_conformance.py` holds both engines to this.

A model declaration describes a typed call; it does not create a provider.
The host MUST supply a binding for each model reachable from the selected
workflow before execution. A direct `use_model` call sends the input record to
that provider and accepts only a complete, strict JSON result matching the
declared output record.

`output: NAME as text` declares a model that answers in plain text. NAME
MUST be a record with exactly one field, of type Text. The model is asked
for the text alone, not JSON; when the answer holds one fenced code block,
the lines inside it are the text, and otherwise the whole answer, trimmed.
That text is the field's value. A small model writes a whole file far
better as itself than escaped inside a JSON string. The trace keeps the
answer as the model gave it, marked `plain`, and replay reads it the same
way. `kosika-native` does not read such a model yet.

"""Tests written in Kosika.

A program may hold tests next to the code they exercise:

    test "a double charge goes to billing" {
      answers assistant: [{label: "billing", confidence: 0.9}]
      result = main({text: "My card was charged twice."})
      expect result.queue == "billing"
    }

A test body is a list of lines, run in order:

`answers MODEL: [record, ...]`
    The answers a declared model gives, in the order it is asked. No real
    model is called by a test. A model with no `answers` line fails the test
    if it is asked anything, and so do answers that were never used.
`name = expression`
    Binds a value. The expression may call a function, or run a workflow by
    calling it like a function.
`expect expression`
    The expression must be `true`.

Tests are not part of the program that runs: `program_payload` leaves them
out, so adding or changing a test never changes a program's hash, its traces,
or its approvals. A test can only reach what a run with scripted models can
reach. It cannot execute a tool.

workflows.
- Use named arguments. Provided argument names and types MUST exactly match the
  declaration.
- Run their body in the order it is written: each `let`, `var`, loop,
  conditional, and assignment executes in turn, and a line may use only names
  declared above it.
- May declare immutable `let` locals and assignable `var` locals. Assignment
  to a `let`, an unknown name, or a value of another type is rejected.
- May declare named nested functions. A nested function may capture lexical
  values. `ref name` creates a typed function value, including its captures,
  and function values may be passed, returned, stored in workflow bindings, and
  called.
- May recurse only when every function participating in the cycle declares
  `recurse N`, where `N` is from 1 through 128. Static function nesting and call
  depth are also bounded at 32.
- MUST end in one `return` expression with the declared output type.
- MAY also return early. `return value` written inside an `if`, a `match`
  arm, or a loop body leaves the innermost enclosing function at once with
  that value, which MUST have the function's output type and is validated
  like the final one. An early return produces no value where it stands, so
  the branch holding it takes the type of the other branch.

There is no implicit coercion. The one mixed arithmetic form is
`Text + Number`, which formats the number and concatenates it to the text.

neither can `extract` into a record with its own field named `evidence`.
- Evidence proves the quoted words were in the input. It does not prove that
  they support the answer.
- A model step (`use_model` or a thinking step) MAY be followed by `retry N`,
  with N from 1 to 5, written after the call and before any `otherwise`:
  `label = classify t.text into ["a", "b"] with evidence retry 2 otherwise f(t)`.
  When the model's answer is rejected (it is not valid for the record, breaks
  a thinking-step guarantee, or lacks evidence), the model is asked again and
  shown its rejected answer and the reason, up to N more times. Only a
  rejected answer is retried; a provider failure is not. Every attempt counts
  as a model call for the limits. When the retries are used up, the step
  fails as it would have, so its `otherwise` runs. Rejected answers and their
  reasons are kept in the trace.

- A model step MAY be followed by `verify CHECK(arguments)`, written after
  the call and before any `vote` or `retry`:
  `found = use_model reader(p.text) verify proven(found, hits) retry 1`.
  CHECK MUST be a function declared in the program that returns Text. Its
  arguments may use the step's own name, which holds the model's answer, and
  the values of earlier steps. It is called on every answer that is
  otherwise acceptable. A result other than `""` rejects the answer with
  that text as the reason, exactly as a malformed answer is rejected, so
  `retry` and `otherwise` apply unchanged. The check of the accepted answer
  is kept in the trace, and replay requires it to be well formed and to
  have returned `""`. A `match` step and a step that is not a model step
  MUST NOT have `verify`.

  the reason as Text. `try { BODY } retry N otherwise { OTHER }` evaluates
  BODY up to N more times first. BODY and OTHER MUST have the same type.

- A step MAY be a plain value, worked out by code: `count = before + 1`,
  `big = if count > 3 { true } else { false }`, `tally = {count: count}`.
  A call followed by more of an expression on its line, as `shout =
  base(m) + 1`, is a value too. Its type is, in this order: the type
  written out, `typed: Tally = {count: n}`; the type of the value itself;
  the parameter or tool input field it is handed to whole by a later step,

def _entry_point_error(program: Program, workflow_name: str) -> str:
    """Explain a missing entry point, including when a swarm is the real reason.

    A program whose only entry point is a declared swarm has nothing to run.
    Reporting ``Unknown workflow 'main'`` there is worse than unhelpful: it reads
    as a forgotten ``main`` and sends the reader looking for the wrong bug. The
    swarm is the honest answer, so the error says so and names what can be run.
    """

    if program.swarms:
        names = ", ".join(sorted(swarm.name for swarm in program.swarms))
        available = sorted(workflow.name for workflow in program.workflows)
        entry = (
            f"This program declares swarm(s) {names}, and a declared swarm is a "
            "statement of intent rather than an executable entry point. Kosika "
            "does not execute swarms yet, so there is nothing to run for "
            f"{workflow_name!r}."
        )
        if available:
            entry += f" Runnable workflow(s): {', '.join(available)}."
        else:
            entry += " This program declares no workflow to run."
        return entry
    return f"Unknown workflow {workflow_name!r}"

# Kosika: what it is, how it is built, and why

Written 10 October 2026. Every number here was measured on this project and
can be re-run; where something is not proven, it says so.

## What Kosika is

- **A programming language for building AI agents.** You write a `.kos`
  file that says what the agent is given, what it may use, which steps it
  takes, and what it must give back.
- **A language where asking a model is a built-in step,** not a library
  call. `use_model`, `classify`, `summarize`, `extract` and `decide` are
  words of the language, and their answers are checked for shape before the
  next step sees them.
- **A language that separates asking from granting.** A program can only
  ask for a folder, a website, a model or the right to start a program.
  The person who runs it grants each one, and anything that changes the
... (lines left out) ...

What it is not, today:

- It is not a finished product. It is a working prototype used by one
  person on one laptop.
- It is not its own engine. Kosika programs are run by a program written
  in Python.
- It does not make a model smarter. It makes a program refuse, retry, or
  ask a stronger model when an answer does not pass a check you wrote.

## How it is being built

10. **K11 — Approval-controlled AI changes.** Apply exact checked proposals only
    after authenticated host review; resolve workflow-agent mutation integration.
11. **K12 — Reproducible delivery (local slice exercised).** Build wheel and
    source artifacts containing the CLI, LSP, and workbench assets; install the
    wheel outside the checkout; and smoke check, run, replay, LSP, and workbench.
    Published releases and remote execution remain planned.

**Active task: K10c.** K10b (below) made one swarm invocable under a one-use
approval with deterministic rounds and an aggregate budget. K10c is what K10b
left out: typed messages between members, state carried from one round to the
next, and a termination judgment over observed evidence rather than result
equality. Swarm output must not acquire authority the way model output cannot.

- **One-line steps.** Inside a workflow, `name = call` is a step. The parser
  expands it to the long form, so both produce the same tree and nothing

- **Short arguments.** `f(order)` means `f(order: order)` and `f(question.text)`
  means `f(text: question.text)`. The name is read from the expression, never
  guessed; any other expression must be named (`parse/unnamed-argument`).
- **"Did you mean" hints** on unknown variables, fields, record fields,
  argument names, methods, method arguments, and unknown type or function
  names, from the closest known spelling (`difflib`, cutoff 0.7). No hint is
  printed when nothing is close.
- Errors in a one-line step anchor to that line.

  `environment NAME { ... }` for each way it runs: `model NAME: "..." at

  calls, N tool calls, N seconds` and `keep "folder"`.
- `kosika run --env NAME` (kosika/environment.py) and `kosika-native run
  --env NAME` (native/env.go) find the file beside the program or above
  it and take everything from it. The options it decides (`--model`,
  `--mcp-server`, `--allow-folder`, `--journal` and the rest) are refused

equal a field of the record, MUST NOT be `get`, `has`, `set`, `remove`,

- A workflow step MAY be `read file PATH`, `list files PATH`,

  built-in `system "files"` or `system "web"` tool (`file_read`, `file_list`,
  `file_write`, `web_fetch`) with built-in records `FileContent {text}`,
  `FileNames {names}`, `FileSaved {bytes}` and `WebPage {url, title, text}`.
  All the rules of those tools apply: the host MUST grant the folder or
  site, and `write file` is an `execute` tool, so its workflow MUST say

- A model step MAY be followed by `verify CHECK(arguments)`, written after
  the call and before any `vote` or `retry`:
  `found = use_model reader(p.text) verify proven(found, hits) retry 1`.
  CHECK MUST be a function declared in the program that returns Text. Its
  arguments may use the step's own name, which holds the model's answer, and
  the values of earlier steps. It is called on every answer that is
  otherwise acceptable. A result other than `""` rejects the answer with
  that text as the reason, exactly as a malformed answer is rejected, so
  `retry` and `otherwise` apply unchanged. The check of the accepted answer
  is kept in the trace, and replay requires it to be well formed and to
  have returned `""`. A `match` step and a step that is not a model step

records, functions (nested ones, closures, recursion within a stated
depth), `if`, `match`, `for`, `while`, `repeat`, `try`, `fail`, text with

one in a folder named `assistant`. While an agent works you watch it. Each

shows what the agent remembers, entry by entry. The other tabs show every

The Map tab is the place to start with an agent you do not know. It says
what the agent is for, what you give it and get back, what it only looks
at, what it may change (always after asking you), which models it asks,
what it remembers, and what it does in order; a step that runs another
workflow opens to show that workflow's steps. Every item says where it
comes from: "from the program" with its line, "from the comment at the
top of the file", or "written by a person". Kosika never guesses a
purpose: if there is no comment, the map says none is written, and you can
save one sentence of your own, kept in `purpose.txt` beside the program.
Where the agent reaches something Kosika cannot look inside, such as a
program it starts or an outside server, the map says so. No model writes
any part of the map.

`agent.can` is the enforced tool allow-list. Every listed capability MUST name
a declared tool. `agent.cannot` records explicit denial and MUST NOT overlap
`can`; it does not widen authority. An agent used by `ask` MUST name a declared
model. Its provider sees only tools in `can`.

Agent defaults and bounds:

| Field | Default | Allowed |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `max_steps` | 8 | 1–64 |
| `max_tool_calls` | 256 | 1–1,000,000 |
| `max_model_calls` | 64 | 1–1,000,000 |
| `deadline_seconds` | none | greater than 0 and at most 86,400 |

Declarations are requests for authority, never authority themselves. The host
MUST bind declared providers and tools explicitly. Bindings for undeclared
models or tools are rejected, and reachable capabilities are preflighted
before the first workflow step executes.

## Fundamentals: early return and `if` without `else` (complete)

- `return value` may appear inside an `if`, `match` arm, or loop body
  (`ReturnExpr`). The checker gives it the type `Never`, requires its value to
  fit the enclosing function's output type, and rejects it outside a function.
  The runtime unwinds to the function and validates the value like the final
  return. Recursion detection sees calls made in an early return.
- `if condition { ... }` with no `else` has `null` as its other branch, so it
  is a do-nothing statement or an optional value.
- A function still ends with a final `return`, so a body cannot fall off its
  end without a value.

## Fundamentals: `otherwise` (complete)

- `step = call otherwise fallback` gives a step one fallback call
  (`Step.fallback`, absent from the hashed payload when unset).
- Runtime: the step loop is now a queue. A recoverable failure discards the
  step's partial events, marks a durable step as not started, and queues the
  same step with the fallback as its call. The retried step's `step_start`
  event carries `recovered_from`, so traces keep their four-events-per-step
  shape and trace version 5 replay is unchanged.
- Recoverable: `RuntimeError` and `ValueError` raised by the step's work.
  Never recovered: `ExecutionError` (budget, deadline, cancellation),
  `ApprovalRequiredError`, and `PermissionError` (missing bindings).

`ui/kosika.css` is the single source of truth for Kosika's interface. The SVG renderer in
`kosika/design.py` mirrors the same palette, so a diagram the engine generates and a surface a
human reads share one visual language.

**Structure is cyan, intelligence is violet, authority is amber.** A colour is never decoration. If
you cannot name the meaning of a hue in one word, it does not get one.

diagram is flat. If everything glows, nothing is live.

**Numbers are monospaced and tabular.** Digests, sequence numbers, line counts, hashes, positions.
Alignment is information.

## Language and runtime expansion

Kosika includes local imports with explicit exports, typed workflow calls, pure
functions, closures, higher-order values, bounded loops and recursion, nested
replay, model budgets/telemetry, durable checkpoints and approval pauses, a
bounded read-only DAG API, host-granted JSON/HTTP/SQLite adapters, development
commands, an LSP/editor backend, and evaluation fixtures.

See [DEVELOPMENT.md](DEVELOPMENT.md) for runnable examples, APIs, security
boundaries, and current limitations. Live provider bindings exist but a working
model endpoint is environment-dependent and has not been established as a
release guarantee. Parallel DAG execution is a host API rather than language
swarm execution. Editor/LSP integration is implemented but not equivalent to a
packaged, production-tested IDE experience.

- A model step (`use_model` or a thinking step) MAY be followed by `retry N`,
  with N from 1 to 5, written after the call and before any `otherwise`:
  `label = classify t.text into ["a", "b"] with evidence retry 2 otherwise f(t)`.
  When the model's answer is rejected (it is not valid for the record, breaks
  a thinking-step guarantee, or lacks evidence), the model is asked again and
  shown its rejected answer and the reason, up to N more times. Only a
  rejected answer is retried; a provider failure is not. Every attempt counts
  as a model call for the limits. When the retries are used up, the step
  fails as it would have, so its `otherwise` runs. Rejected answers and their
  reasons are kept in the trace.

- A model step MAY be followed by `vote N`, with N one of 3, 5, 7, or 9,
  written after the call and before any `retry`:
  `label = classify t.text into ["a", "b"] vote 3 retry 1 otherwise f(t)`.
  The model is asked N times, and the step succeeds only when more than half
  of the N answers agree. Two answers agree when they give the same label
  (`classify`), the same answer (`decide`), or the same whole record
  (`extract`, `use_model`). `summarize` cannot vote. The step's value is the
  first answer on the winning side. An answer that is rejected, after its own
  retries, is a vote for nothing. Without a majority the step fails like any
  broken answer, so its `otherwise` runs. Every ask counts as a model call,
  and the tally is kept in the trace.

  module and the program hash. Checking verifies each module's SHA-256,

## Trace and replay semantics

A successful run may write newline-delimited JSON. New runs emit trace version
`5`; offline replay accepts versions `1` through `5`.

Version 5 records:

- Program hash, selected workflow, exact inputs, and output schema.
- Ordered step start, call, return, and completion events.
- Nested workflow event lists.
- Function call/return events, including function calls evaluated inside
  arguments and function bodies.
- Model, agent, and tool input/output schemas and recorded outcomes.
- Final result and cooperative execution counters.

`replay(trace)` is **validated outcome replay**:

- It performs no model, tool, MCP, network, or source-code execution.
- It requires one completed run with ordered, matched events.
- It recursively validates nested workflows and function events.
- It validates recorded arguments and results against recorded schemas.
- It validates model content against its recorded JSON result and validates
  agent transcripts.
- It returns the final recorded result only after those checks pass.

## Python SDK (complete)

- `kosika.sdk` builds a program from Python: `App.record`, `model`, `tool`,
  `agent`, `workflow`, `swarm`, and `source`; workflow steps `use_model`, `ask`,
  `execute`, `call`, and `function`. Step methods return a `Ref` to their
  result so later steps can use it; `ref("question.text")` passes any Kosika
  expression, and Python values become Kosika literals.
- It is a source builder, not a second front end. `to_source()` renders `.kos`
  text and `build()` runs `parse` and `check` on it, so the checker stays the
  only authority and no AST is constructed by hand. `save()` writes a file only
  after the program checks.
- The SDK mints no authority: `run()` forwards explicit bindings to
  `kosika.runtime.run`, and an unbound model fails closed.

## What it has

The core of the language, which reaches nothing outside the program:
records, functions (nested ones, closures, recursion within a stated
depth), `if`, `match`, `for`, `while`, `repeat`, `try`, `fail`, text with
values written in (`f"..."`), and the built-in methods on text, numbers,
lists, maps and optional values. Whole numbers are exact at any size.

Models, with the records they take and give. Workflows, whose steps call
a function, run another workflow, use a tool through an agent, or ask a
model (asked again on a refused answer with `retry`), with a fallback
(`otherwise`) or a choice of call (`match`); tools and agents as they are
declared; and tests that run a workflow and script what its models and
tools answer. A model or a tool is reached only through those scripted
answers: this engine reaches no real one yet, and a tool that changes the
world is refused, as the reference refuses it in a test, for want of a
recorded approval.

Before it runs a program it checks it, as the reference does: a program
whose types do not agree is refused, with the reference's own message, on
the output and with exit code 2. A name the file uses but never declares is
refused as the file is read, like a fault in the text.

## Standard coding-agent procedure

1. Inspect `git status`, the relevant source files, tests, and this plan.
2. State the smallest proposed slice and any assumptions.
3. Implement without discarding unrelated changes.
4. Add focused tests, including failure branches where relevant.
5. Run focused tests.
6. Run the complete quality suite.
7. Review the diff and generated artifacts.
8. Report changed files, quality results, unresolved limitations, and the next slice.

### Default values, and making a record by calling it

- The owner asked for Kosika to match Python's functions, classes and
  attributes, and do better. Agreed order: default values, enums, shapes
  (interfaces), a larger standard library.
- Default values, in both engines (kosika/sugar.py `fill_defaults`,
  native/defaults.go): `fn greet(name: Text, loud: Bool = false)` may be
  called without `loud`, by name or in order; `record Item { count: Number
  = 1 }` gives a field a default, and `Item(name: "pen")` makes an Item, as
  a class is made in Python. A default must be written out and fit its
  type, checked before the program runs. The call is given its defaults
  before anything checks it, so traces, replay and every other part see an
  ordinary call; a program without defaults keeps its tree and its hash.

A `field:` argument MUST be a text literal naming a field of the element
record. The checker resolves it, so a misspelled or wrongly typed field is a
check error rather than a run failure. To sort descending, follow `sort()` or
`sort_by(...)` with `reverse()`.
| any `T?` | `or(default: T)` | `T`: the value, or the default when absent |
| any `T?` | `exists()` | `Bool` |
| any `T?` | `value()` | `T`; fails the run when absent |
| any `T{}` | `get(key: Text)` | `T?` |
| any `T{}` | `has(key: Text)` | `Bool` |
| any `T{}` | `set(key: Text, value: T)`, `remove(key: Text)` | a new map; the receiver is never changed. A result over 4,096 entries fails the run |
| any `T{}` | `keys()`, `values()`, `length()` | `Text[]`, `T[]`, `Number` |

An optional value has only `or`, `exists`, and `value`: its own methods and
fields are reached after one of those. A map has no fields. A map literal is
written like a record literal, with quoted or bare keys (`{"north": 4}`), and
needs a map type from its context; `{}` is the empty map.
| array of `Text`, `Number`, or `Bool` | `contains(item: T)` | `Bool`, using `==` |
| `Number` | `floor()`, `ceil()`, `round()` | whole `Number`; `round` rounds halves up |

`slice` positions MUST be whole numbers with `0 <= start <= end <= length`;
anything else fails the run.

An unknown method or wrong argument name is a check error
(`check/unknown-method`, `check/method-arguments`). A parenthesised literal is
needed to call a method on a number literal: `(2.5).round()`.

## How Kosika compares with Python

`kosika compare-python` runs six tasks written three ways: Kosika, short
"plain" Python, and "checked" Python that also rejects wrongly shaped data.
All three return the same answers. Measured on these six tasks:

| | Kosika | Python, plain | Python, checked |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lines of code, all six tasks | 103 | 81 | 108, plus 35 shared helper lines |
| Lines, four data tasks | 69 | 38 | 47 |
| Lines, two model tasks | 34 | 43 | 61 |
| Bad-data cases refused, of 20 | 20 | 9 | 20 |

Kosika is longer than plain Python for ordinary data handling, and shorter
once a model is involved. Its advantage is not size: it refuses every bad case
without extra code, where plain Python silently accepted 11 of 20, such as a
label the model invented or `true` where a number belongs. The bad cases were
chosen by the author of the comparison, so read that column as "what Kosika
checks for free", not as an unbiased error rate. Details and limits are in
[KOSIKA_PLAN.md](KOSIKA_PLAN.md).

For an agent that plans first, every `execute` call its model requests in one
reply forms its plan. The host is asked once, with the whole ordered list of
tools and arguments, before any of them runs; the approval is bound to exactly
that list. The calls then run in order and stop at the first failure. An
`execute` call requested in a later reply MUST NOT run; the model is told so
as that call's result. When the step is resumed after approval the model's
earlier replies are replayed from the run's journal, not requested again.

A host MAY supply skills to a run. Before an `ask` step the runtime selects,
without a model, the skills whose trigger words occur in the step's text
arguments, at most three. Selected skills are appended to the agent's system
text and listed in the `agent_call` trace event as `skills`, each with an `id`
and the reason it was selected. Skills MUST NOT change which tools an agent
can reach or what requires approval.

Declarations are requests for authority, never authority themselves. The host
MUST bind declared providers and tools explicitly. Bindings for undeclared
models or tools are rejected, and reachable capabilities are preflighted
before the first workflow step executes.

A tool whose source is `system` asks for access to the machine the program
runs on. It adds no new statement: it is a tool, used with `execute`.

| `classify text into choices` | `Choice {label: Text, confidence: Number}`; the label is always one of the choices |
| `extract Record from text` | your own record `Record` |
| `summarize text` | `Summary {text: Text}` |

- Do not declare `Choice`, `Summary`, or `Decision` yourself; they are built in.
  Use them as parameter types: `fn route(label: Choice, refund: Decision)`.
- With more than one model, end the step with `using model_name`.
- Add `with evidence` to `classify`, `extract`, or `decide` to make the model
  quote the text: `invoice = extract Invoice from ticket.text with evidence`.
  An answer whose quote is not in the text is rejected. With `extract`, make
  fields that may be missing optional (`amount: Number?`).

It can reach only the tools in `can`, and only as far as the person running

Today there are two engines: the reference engine in `kosika/` (Python)
and the native engine in `native/` (Go). The native engine exists so that
Kosika can run on a machine with no Python.

## What is here

    cases/NAME.kos             a program whose tests must all pass
    cases/NAME.expected.txt    what `test` prints for it
    failing/NAME.kos           a program whose tests fail on purpose
    failing/NAME.expected.txt  what `test` prints for it, failures and all
    refused/NAME.kos           a program the checker must refuse
    refused/NAME.expected.txt  the one line `test` prints for it

Every program here gives the same result on any machine. It asks no
model and reaches no file; where a workflow uses a tool, the test scripts
what the tool answers.

## What an engine must do

For each `.kos` file, `ENGINE test FILE` must print exactly the text in
the file beside it, and end with exit code 0 when every test passed, 1
when one failed, and 2 when the program was refused before it ran. A
refused program prints `Check failed: ` and the reason, and nothing else. Line ends may be `\n` or `\r\n`.

An engine must also split every `.kos` file in this repository into the
same tokens as the reference: `ENGINE tokens FILE` prints one JSON object
a line, `{"kind", "value", "line", "column"}`.

workflows.
- Use named arguments. Provided argument names and types MUST exactly match the
  declaration.
- Run their body in the order it is written: each `let`, `var`, loop,
  conditional, and assignment executes in turn, and a line may use only names
  declared above it.
- May declare immutable `let` locals and assignable `var` locals. Assignment
  to a `let`, an unknown name, or a value of another type is rejected.
- May declare named nested functions. A nested function may capture lexical
  values. `ref name` creates a typed function value, including its captures,
  and function values may be passed, returned, stored in workflow bindings, and
  called.
- May recurse only when every function participating in the cycle declares
  `recurse N`, where `N` is from 1 through 32. Static function nesting and call
  depth are also bounded at 32.
- MUST end in one `return` expression with the declared output type.
- MAY also return early. `return value` written inside an `if`, a `match`
  arm, or a loop body leaves the innermost enclosing function at once with
  that value, which MUST have the function's output type and is validated
  like the final one. An early return produces no value where it stands, so
  the branch holding it takes the type of the other branch.

### Talking to a program

## What it has

The core of the language, which reaches nothing outside the program:
records, functions (nested ones, closures, recursion within a stated
depth), `if`, `match`, `for`, `while`, `repeat`, `try`, `fail`, text with
values written in (`f"..."`), and the built-in methods on text, numbers,
lists, maps and optional values. Whole numbers are exact at any size.

Models, with the records they take and give, and general ones that take
and give text. Workflows, whose steps call
a function, run another workflow, use a tool through an agent, or ask a
model (asked again on a refused answer with `retry`), ask an agent, or
think (`classify`, `extract`, `summarize`, `decide`), with a fallback
(`otherwise`) or a choice of call (`match`); tools and agents as they are
declared; and tests that run a workflow and script what its models and
tools answer. With `run`, a model is a real one: a model server spoken to
as the reference speaks to it, with the same requests word for word; a
tool is answered by a pinned MCP server; and an agent's model may call the
agent's tools, each answer given back to it, until it answers. A tool that
changes the world is refused, as the reference refuses it without a
recorded approval.

Before it runs a program it checks it, as the reference does: a program
whose types do not agree is refused, with the reference's own message, on
the output and with exit code 2. A name the file uses but never declares is
refused as the file is read, like a fault in the text.

Kosika starts that command itself, never through a shell, and keeps the
server running while Studio is open. The Tools page lists every granted
server with the tools it offers, and for each tool the Kosika text to paste
into a program. An agent given such tools in its `can` list is told what
they do in the server's own words and chooses among them.

The Skills page lists the skills kept beside each agent, in its `skills`
folder: what each is for, the words that pick it, and the rules it holds
files to. Type a request there to see which skills it would pick, and
why; no model is asked. A skill can be changed or a new one written on
the page. One that Kosika cannot read is not saved, and the page says why.

## Kosika without Python

`native/` holds a second engine, written in Go, that builds to one program
file and runs the core of Kosika (records, functions and tests) on a
machine with no Python. `conformance/` holds the programs both engines
must agree on, with what each must print. The native engine has no checker
and no workflows, agents, tools or models yet; see `native/README.md` for
what it has and what it lacks.

A tool may be `access: observe` only when the server itself marks it
read-only. Any other tool must be `access: execute`, so each use waits for
your Allow once. A tool that answers in plain text needs an output record
with one Text field. `examples/mcp` has a small notes server and an agent,
`librarian.kos`, that uses it.

A granted server runs with your authority. Grant only servers you trust.

### 2. Program Distribution System

**Program Package Format (.kosika):**

- The body is `let`/`var` declarations and statements, run in the order they
  are written, then exactly one `return expression` as the last line. There is
  no early return.
- `let` cannot be reassigned. Use `var` for a value you assign later.
- Operators: `+ - * / %`, `< <= > >=`, `== !=`, `and`, `or`, `not`.
  `Text + Text` and `Text + Number` join text. There is no `&&`, `||`, or `!`.
  `/` always gives a fraction (`7 / 2` is `3.5`); use `(7 / 2).floor()` for a
  whole number, for example as an array index.
- There are no free built-in functions (no `len(x)`), but there are built-in
  methods, all with named arguments:

| On | Methods |
| --- | --- |
| `Text` | `length()`, `upper()`, `lower()`, `trim()`, `contains(part: t)`, `starts_with(prefix: t)`, `ends_with(suffix: t)`, `split(separator: t)` |
| any array | `length()`; `contains(item: x)` for arrays of Text, Number, or Bool |
| `Text[]` | `join(separator: t)` |
| `Number` | `floor()`, `ceil()`, `round()` |

  Arrays cannot be changed in place: there is no `push`. Build a new array
  with a `for` expression.

- **A language that separates asking from granting.** A program can only
  ask for a folder, a website, a model or the right to start a program.
  The person who runs it grants each one, and anything that changes the
  outside world waits for a yes to that exact action.
- **A set of tools around the language:**
  - a checker that finds mistakes before anything runs;
  - a test runner with scripted model answers, so tests need no model;
  - `kosika measure`, which runs the same questions on real models and
    reports how many each gets right and how long it takes;
  - a trace of every run that can be replayed without the model;
  - Kosika Studio, a desktop-style app to see agents, run them, watch each
    step, and approve their actions.
- **Eight example agents written in it:** researcher, planner, coach,
  doctor, workbench, scout, author (an agent that writes Kosika), and
  animator (motion designs from a description).

What it is not, today:

- It is not a finished product. It is a working prototype used by one
  person on one laptop.
- It is not its own engine. Kosika programs are run by a program written
  in Python.
- It does not make a model smarter. It makes a program refuse, retry, or
  ask a stronger model when an answer does not pass a check you wrote.

- The call is one of:
  - `some_function(arg: value)`

  - `ask agent_name(field: value)` runs the agent's model with its tools; the

- Later steps can use the names bound by earlier steps and the parameters.
- The last step's result must have the workflow's result type.
- Put any logic in a `fn` and call it from a step.

  model answer: `label = classify t.text into ["a", "b"] otherwise
  keyword_label(t)`. Both calls must return the same type. Not allowed on
  `access: execute` tools.
- A workflow can cap its own run with a line such as
  `budget 6 model calls, 30 seconds` (also `tool calls`). Reaching it stops
  the run; `otherwise` does not catch it.
- If a step executes a tool whose access is `execute`, the workflow must end
  with the line `require approval` after its last step.

  applies as for any failure.

  first parameter MUST be written `self` and has the record's type. The
  function is called as `VALUE.NAME(arguments)` on a value of that record
  and is otherwise an ordinary function, named `Record$NAME`. NAME MUST NOT
  equal a field of the record, MUST NOT be `get`, `has`, `set`, `remove`,
  `keys`, `values` or `length`, and two records with exactly the same field
  names MUST NOT both declare the same NAME. There is no inheritance. A
  record with no functions is unchanged and keeps its hash.

- A workflow step MAY be `read file PATH`, `list files PATH`,
  `write file PATH with TEXT`, or `fetch URL`. Each stands for a call to a
  built-in `system "files"` or `system "web"` tool (`file_read`, `file_list`,

  All the rules of those tools apply: the host MUST grant the folder or
  site, and `write file` is an `execute` tool, so its workflow MUST say
  `require approval`. They MUST NOT appear inside a `fn`.

- Arrays built by methods may hold 1,000,000 elements (was 4,096), maps
  100,000 entries (was 4,096), and `recurse N` and the call depth go to 128
  (was 32). Replay accepts the same depth.
- 128 is measured, not chosen: the Python-hosted interpreter fails between
  200 and 250 nested calls, so 128 leaves room for deep expressions.
- Not claimed: deep recursion. An algorithm that needs thousands of nested

- A system tool MUST declare `access: execute`, and its records MUST have
  exactly the fields above (`check/invalid-system-tool`). A workflow that
  executes one therefore MUST state `require approval`.
- Declaring a system tool grants nothing. The host binds files tools only when
  it grants a folder, and shell tools only when it also allows shell. An
  unbound system tool fails the run before its first step.
- Every call needs its own approval for that exact tool and arguments, through
  the same session and ledger as any other `execute` tool.
- A shell tool starts only the program named in `operation`, with `args`
  passed as a list and never interpreted by a shell, inside the granted
  folder, for at most 60 seconds, with output cut at 64 KiB per stream.
- `search` gives the lines holding the query's words and `find` the lines
  nearest to it in meaning, each as `path:line: text`, best first. Both
  only read and MAY be declared `access: observe`. `find` gives at most
  12 lines, compares at most 4,000 lines of at least 12 characters, and
  is bound only when the host also grants an embedding model

  tool. The host keeps what the embedding model returns for each line

- **A language that separates asking from granting.** A program can only
  ask for a folder, a website, a model or the right to start a program.
  The person who runs it grants each one, and anything that changes the
  outside world waits for a yes to that exact action.
- **A set of tools around the language:**
  - a checker that finds mistakes before anything runs;
  - a test runner with scripted model answers, so tests need no model;
  - `kosika measure`, which runs the same questions on real models and
    reports how many each gets right and how long it takes;
  - a trace of every run that can be replayed without the model;
  - Kosika Studio, a desktop-style app to see agents, run them, watch each
    step, and approve their actions.
- **Ten example agents written in it:** researcher, planner, coach,
  doctor, workbench, scout, builder (shows its whole plan before it makes
  any file), coder (does a small task in a Python project and runs the
  tests), author (an agent that writes Kosika), and animator (motion
  designs from a description).

What it is not, today:

- It is not a finished product. It is a working prototype used by one
  person on one laptop.
- It is not its own engine. Kosika programs are run by a program written
  in Python.
- It does not make a model smarter. It makes a program refuse, retry, or

## What it has

The core of the language, which reaches nothing outside the program:
records, functions (nested ones, closures, recursion within a stated
depth), `if`, `match`, `for`, `while`, `repeat`, `try`, `fail`, text with
values written in (`f"..."`), and the built-in methods on text, numbers,
lists, maps and optional values. Whole numbers are exact at any size.

Models, with the records they take and give, and general ones that take
and give text. Workflows, whose steps call
a function, run another workflow, use a tool through an agent, or ask a
model (asked again on a refused answer with `retry`), or think
(`classify`, `extract`, `summarize`, `decide`), with a fallback
(`otherwise`) or a choice of call (`match`); tools and agents as they are
declared; and tests that run a workflow and script what its models and
tools answer. A model or a tool is reached only through those scripted
answers: this engine reaches no real one yet, and a tool that changes the
world is refused, as the reference refuses it in a test, for want of a
recorded approval.

Before it runs a program it checks it, as the reference does: a program
whose types do not agree is refused, with the reference's own message, on
the output and with exit code 2. A name the file uses but never declares is
refused as the file is read, like a fault in the text.

## What it does not have yet

- Steps with `verify`, `vote`, `escalate` or `with evidence`, and
  `parallel` blocks.
- An agent's plan that writes files, or an agent with its own `check`:
  the reference checks such a plan before showing it, and those checks are
  not here yet, so such a plan is refused by name. Replaying an agent
  run's own trace, an answer with evidence, or a verified answer.
- Reaching a real tool other than through an MCP server: `system` tools,
  files, pages, the clock and chance. So an environment's `allow folder`,
  `allow shell` and `allow site` are read but grant nothing here yet.
- Swarms and imports.
- A file that has any of these is refused, and the refusal names it.
- Vectors and matrices.

  with no deadline. Hosts MAY lower or raise each count from 1 through
  1,000,000 and MAY set a positive deadline.

  and provider/tool calls. They do not preempt an in-flight host effect.

A host MAY supply skills to a run. Before an `ask` step the runtime selects
at most three: first the skills whose trigger words occur in the step's text
arguments, then any the agent's model names when shown the list of skills. A
name that is not a supplied skill is ignored. The selection is journaled, so
a resumed step uses the same skills. Selected skills are appended to the agent's system
text and listed in the `agent_call` trace event as `skills`, each with an `id`
and the reason it was selected. Skills MUST NOT change which tools an agent
can reach or what requires approval.

  the call and before any `vote` or `retry`:

  the values of earlier steps. It is called on every answer that is
  otherwise acceptable. A result other than `""` rejects the answer with

## Standard coding-agent procedure

1. Inspect `git status`, the relevant source files, tests, and this plan.
2. State the smallest proposed slice and any assumptions.
3. Implement without discarding unrelated changes.
4. Add focused tests, including failure branches where relevant.
5. Run focused tests.
6. Run the complete quality suite.
7. Review the diff and generated artifacts.
8. Report changed files, quality results, unresolved limitations, and the next slice.

## Definition of done for a slice

It is held to the conformance suite in `../conformance`, where it must
print what the reference engine prints, word for word. See
`tests/test_conformance.py`.

- Steps with `verify`, `vote`, `escalate` or `with evidence`, and
  `parallel` blocks.
- An agent's plan that writes files, or an agent with its own `check`:
  the reference checks such a plan before showing it, and those checks are
  not here yet, so such a plan is refused by name. Replaying an agent
  run's own trace, an answer with evidence, or a verified answer.
- Reaching a real tool other than through an MCP server: `system` tools,
  files and pages. So an environment's `allow folder`,
  `allow shell` and `allow site` are read but grant nothing here yet.
- Swarms.
- A file that has any of these is refused, and the refusal names it.

### The native engine checks evidence

- `classify`, `extract` and `decide` written `with evidence` run in
  native/ (native/evidence.go): the model is asked for its answer plus
  quotes, every quote must appear in the text the step was given
  (ignoring case, spacing and curly quotation marks, after NFKC and
  casefolding as the reference does), and an answer whose quote is not
  there is refused like any other, so `retry` and `otherwise` apply. The
  quotes are kept in the trace and proved again on replay, by either
  engine.
- The engine's first outside package: `golang.org/x/text`, for NFKC and
  full case folding, which Go's standard library lacks. It is vendored
  (3.4 MB), so the engine still builds with no network.

- **With an outside agent**, it is as able as that agent on small tasks,

  changed, and all of them if it finds none. A change that breaks a test
  named after something else is not seen until all are run.

### Built-in methods

A method call is `value.method(name: argument)`. The set is closed: there are
no user-defined methods and records have none. The checker resolves a call from
the receiver's type, and every method is pure and deterministic.

| Receiver | Method | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Text` | `length()` | `Number` of characters |
| `Text` | `upper()`, `lower()`, `trim()` | `Text` |
| `Text` | `contains(part: Text)`, `starts_with(prefix: Text)`, `ends_with(suffix: Text)` | `Bool` |
| `Text` | `split(separator: Text)` | `Text[]`; the separator MUST be non-empty and a result over 512 parts fails the run |
| `Text[]` | `join(separator: Text)` | `Text` |
| `Text` | `capitalize()`, `title()`, `reverse()` | `Text`: the first letter of the text, or of each word, upper case and the rest lower; the characters backwards |
| `Text` | `count(part: Text)`, `repeat(times: Number)` | `Number` of times a non-empty part appears, not overlapping; `Text` repeated a whole number of times |
| `Text` | `add_days(days: Number)`, `days_until(other: Text)`, `weekday()` | for a date written `YYYY-MM-DD`, as `now` gives one: the date that many whole days later, the whole days to another date, and its weekday's name; any other text fails the run |
| `Number` | `clamp(low: Number, high: Number)` | the number, kept from `low` through `high`; `low` above `high` fails the run |
| `Number` | `log()`, `exp()`, `to_fixed(digits: Number)` | the natural logarithm of a number above zero and `e` to a power, rounded to nine places; `Text` with 0 to 20 digits after the point |
| `T[]` | `count(item: T)` | `Number` of items equal to `item` |
| any array | `length()` | `Number` of elements |
| any array | `set(key: Number, value: T)` | a new array with that position replaced |
| `Number` | `to(end: Number)`, `until(end: Number)` | `Number[]` of whole numbers through, or up to, the end |
| any array | `append(item: T)`, `concat(other: T[])`, `reverse()`, `slice(start: Number, end: Number)` | a new array of the same type; the receiver is never changed. A result over 1,000,000 elements fails the run |
| `Text` | `slice(start: Number, end: Number)` | `Text` from position `start` up to, not including, `end` |

## Standard coding-agent procedure

1. Inspect `git status`, the relevant source files, tests, and this plan.
2. State the smallest proposed slice and any assumptions.
3. Implement without discarding unrelated changes.
4. Add focused tests, including failure branches where relevant.
5. Run focused tests.
6. Run the complete quality suite.
7. Review the diff and generated artifacts.
8. Report changed files, quality results, unresolved limitations, and the next slice.

asked for the record plus quotes; `kosika/evidence.py` checks every quote
  against the step's input text and rejects the answer otherwise. The failure
  is an ordinary broken answer, so `otherwise` recovers from it.

  `model_return` trace event, and replay verifies them again from the recorded
  input, so a trace cannot claim evidence its input does not contain.

- Not claimed: a quote proves the words were in the input, not that they

  cannot read the quotes yet; they are in the trace only. Traces with
  evidence are not readable by an older Kosika (they fail closed).

# Kosika for AI authors

Everything needed to write a correct Kosika program. Kosika is its own
language. Do not use Python, JavaScript, or Rust syntax.

## Shape of a program

A program is a list of declarations in any order: `record`, `fn`, `model`,
`tool`, `agent`, `workflow`, `swarm`. No semicolons. `//` starts a comment.
The entry point is `workflow main`.

An optional value has only `or`, `exists`, and `value`: its own methods and
fields are reached after one of those, or after a test proves it present.

A test of `name.exists()` narrows `name` from `T?` to `T` wherever the test is
known to have passed:

- in the true branch of `if name.exists() { ... }`, and in the `else` branch
  of `if not name.exists()`;
- with `and`, for every name tested: `if a.exists() and b.exists() { a + b }`;
- on the lines after a guard that always leaves when the value is absent:
  `if not name.exists() { return ... }` (or `break`, or `continue`);
- in the body of `for x in xs where x.exists() { ... }`.

Only a plain name declared with `let`, a parameter, or a loop variable is
narrowed. A `var` is not, because it may be set back to `null`; a field or an
index is not, so bind it to a `let` first. `exists`, `value`, and `or` remain
valid on a narrowed name. Narrowing is a check-time rule only and does not
change what a program computes.

A braced block holds declarations, assignments, and expressions in any order.
An expression followed by another line is a statement whose value is
discarded; the last expression, if any, is the block's value.

A map has no fields. A map literal is
written like a record literal, with quoted or bare keys (`{"north": 4}`), and
needs a map type from its context; `{}` is the empty map.

## Standard coding-agent procedure

1. Inspect `git status`, the relevant source files, tests, and this plan.
2. State the smallest proposed slice and any assumptions.
3. Implement without discarding unrelated changes.
4. Add focused tests, including failure branches where relevant.
5. Run focused tests.
6. Run the complete quality suite.
7. Review the diff and generated artifacts.
8. Report changed files, quality results, unresolved limitations, and the next slice.

Read this before evaluating anything below.

Kosika is an **early prototype**. It is published so the design can be
reviewed and argued with, not because it is ready to depend on.

- **What works today.** A real parser, type checker, and runtime; typed
  records and workflows; declared models, agents, tools, and capabilities;
  approval-gated execution; deterministic mindmaps; and an offline
  trace/replay loop that re-runs a program without touching the network.
- **What does not work yet.** Live model inference, a language server,
  packaging/distribution, parallelism, and general error messages. Several
  features in the tree are declared, checked, and rendered but never executed.
- **[KOSIKA_VISION.md](KOSIKA_VISION.md) is a design target, not a
  description of this codebase.** It describes a much larger language —
  tensors, memory bubbles, personality policies, an extension ecosystem,
  multi-agent consensus. Almost none of that is implemented. It is included
  to show intent and to argue about, not to claim delivery.
- **The version is `0.1.0` and the API is unstable.** Interfaces will change.

If you are evaluating Kosika for real use today, the honest answer is that it
is not there yet. If you are evaluating the *idea* — that an AI system's
authority, evidence, and replayability should be enforced by the language
rather than by convention — the rest of this file is the substance.

A multi-agent knowledge engine that debates problems to grounded answers through adversarial reasoning.

## Architecture

- **Proposer Agent**: Presents an initial solution with evidence
- **Critic Agent**: Challenges the proposal, identifies weaknesses
- **Judge Agents**: Multiple judges evaluate arguments, vote on consensus
- **Constitution**: Five-part rule system governing debate behavior
- **Bounded Execution**: Hard round and cost ceilings, step limits per agent

### Models that answer as text, in the native engine and in tests

- `output: NAME as text` reads, checks and runs in native/: the model is
  asked for plain text, one fenced block is unwrapped, an empty answer is
  refused, and the trace marks the answer `plain` for either engine's
  replay.
- In both engines a test now scripts such a model with its record,
  `answers writer: [{text: "..."}]`, and the model is taken to have said
  that text. Before, the scripted model said the record as JSON, which a
  real model answering as text never does, so its tests could not say
  what it wrote.
- Held by `cases/plain.kos`, `refused/plain_fields.kos`, and a plain step
  in the run whose trace both engines write alike.

A method call is `value.method(name: argument)`. The set is closed: there are
no user-defined methods and records have none. The checker resolves a call from
the receiver's type, and every method is pure and deterministic.

| Receiver | Method | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Text` | `length()` | `Number` of characters |
| `Text` | `upper()`, `lower()`, `trim()` | `Text` |
| `Text` | `contains(part: Text)`, `starts_with(prefix: Text)`, `ends_with(suffix: Text)` | `Bool` |
| `Text` | `split(separator: Text)` | `Text[]`; the separator MUST be non-empty and a result over 512 parts fails the run |
| `Text[]` | `join(separator: Text)` | `Text` |
| any array | `length()` | `Number` of elements |
| any array | `append(item: T)`, `concat(other: T[])`, `reverse()`, `slice(start: Number, end: Number)` | a new array of the same type; the receiver is never changed. A result over 4,096 elements fails the run |
| `Text` | `slice(start: Number, end: Number)` | `Text` from position `start` up to, not including, `end` |
| `Number` | `to_text()` | `Text`, formatted as in `Text + Number` |
| `Number` | `min(other: Number)`, `max(other: Number)` | the smaller or larger of the two |
| `Text` | `to_number()` | `Number?`: the decimal number the trimmed text spells, else `null` |
| any array | `first()`, `last()` | `T?`, `null` for an empty array |
| `Number[]`, `Text[]` | `sort()` | a new array in ascending order; Text sorts by character code |
| array of `Text`, `Number`, or `Bool` | `unique()` | a new array keeping the first of each equal value |
| `Number[]` | `sum()` | `Number`, `0` for an empty array |
| `Number[]` | `min()`, `max()`, `average()` | `Number?`, `null` for an empty array |

| array of records | `sum_by(field: "name")` | `Number`, the total of a `Number` field |

asked for the record plus quotes; `kosika/evidence.py` checks every quote
  against the step's input text and rejects the answer otherwise. The failure
  is an ordinary broken answer, so `otherwise` recovers from it.
- The step's value and type are unchanged. Quotes are stored on the
  `model_return` trace event, and replay verifies them again from the recorded
  input, so a trace cannot claim evidence its input does not contain.
- Programs without `with evidence` keep the same tree and hash.
- 15 tests in `tests/test_evidence.py`, all with scripted answers.
- Not claimed: a quote proves the words were in the input, not that they
  support the answer. A model can quote a real sentence and still conclude
  wrongly. Number values are not compared with their quote. The program
  cannot read the quotes yet; they are in the trace only. Traces with
  evidence are not readable by an older Kosika (they fail closed).

## Reliability: voting (built, not yet measured)

- `vote N` (3, 5, 7, 9) on a model step asks N times and accepts only what
  more than half agree on (`runtime._ask_with_votes`, `Step.votes`). Agreement
  is on the label, the answer, or the whole record. It composes with evidence
  and retry inside each ask, and with `otherwise` when there is no majority.
- The tally and the rejected ballots are stored on the `model_return` event.
- 12 tests in `tests/test_vote.py`.
- Not claimed: no measurement on a live model. Voting cannot help a model run
  without randomness, and agreement between runs of one model is weaker
  evidence than agreement between different models, which is not built.
  Replay keeps the tally but does not re-derive it.

## Standard coding-agent procedure

5. Run focused tests.

8. Report changed files, quality results, unresolved limitations, and the next slice.

    voters: list[tuple[ModelProvider, ModelDecl]],
    arguments: dict[str, Any],
    asked_schema: dict[str, Any],
    *,
    retries: int,
    votes: int,
) -> tuple[dict[str, Any], dict[str, Any]]:
    """`vote N`: ask N times and accept only what more than half agree on.

    Two answers agree when they give the same label (`classify`), the same
    answer (`decide`), or the same record (anything else). A ballot whose
    answer is rejected counts as a vote for nothing. The step's value is the
    first answer on the winning side. When the step lists several models,
    they take turns: ballot 1 asks the first, ballot 2 the second, and so on.
    """

    provider, model = voters[0]
    if votes == 0:
